claims.text: Yakitori-style chicken is served with tare (a soy-based glaze that standardly contains wheat); this is core to the menu.

name: 土佐料理とおばんざい 柚のす (Tosa Ryori to Obanzai Yunosu)

claims.text: Signature dishes are seasoned with ponzu and soy sauce (e.g., bonito tataki), and standard Japanese soy sauce contains wheat.
The kitchen is fish- and dashi-centered (bonito tataki, bonito-flake croquettes, dashi egg), so animal-derived stock is used broadly across dishes including sides.

name: 十割り蕎麦 つるや (Towari Soba Tsuruya)

claims.text: No gluten-free or cross-contamination protocol is documented; although the soba is 100% buckwheat, it is prepared in a shared kitchen and served with a soy-sauce/dashi broth.
The soba broth/tsuyu is a standard dashi-and-soy-sauce style stock (warm broth, dipping tsuyu), which normally contains wheat-based soy sauce; no wheat-free soy sauce is mentioned.
The kitchen works with chicken and beef and a poultry/dashi-based broth, so vegan cross-contact is likely; no vegan accommodation is documented.
The noodles themselves are 100% buckwheat (juwari) with no wheat flour blended in, which is unusual and relevant for those reducing wheat in the noodle (though the broth is not wheat-free).
As a traditional sushi house, dishes are served and seasoned with standard soy sauce, which contains wheat; no wheat-free soy sauce is documented.
The kitchen is built around fresh fish and seafood, and Japanese sides are typically made with fish dashi, so vegan diners face pervasive animal-product contact.

name: 鶴屋徳満 奈良三条店 (Tsuruya Tokuman Nara Sanjo-ten)

claims.text: A wheat-flour environment: baked goods such as dorayaki/mikasa are made with wheat flour on-site, so flour is present and cross-contact with any flour-free items cannot be ruled out.

Eggs and honey are used in the signature dorayaki/mikasa and the premises also handle bean-paste-only and kuromitsu/kinako sweets; shared utensils and surfaces mean cross-contact between egg-containing and plant-based items is plausible. No vegan separation is documented.

Several items are inherently plant-based by tradition (adzuki bean paste, kanten, kuromitsu black-sugar syrup, kinako soybean flour over shaved ice), giving vegans some workable choices if they confirm ingredients per item.

name: ユーズ・キッチン (U's kitchen)

claims.text: The entire menu is built on house-made wheat pasta, so flour is central to the kitchen; there is no gluten-free preparation or separate workflow documented.
Sauces lean heavily on cream, meat sauce, bacon, scallop, chicken and shrimp, so meat- and dairy-free cooking is not a focus and shared pots are likely.

name: うどん そば 呑み処 三条坊 (Udon Soba Nomidokoro Sanjobo)

claims.text: The kitchen centers on wheat udon and soba cooked in shared water, with no gluten-free menu or allergen labeling shown, so cross-contamination with wheat is effectively unavoidable.
Broths and sauces use standard dashi and seasonings; no wheat-free soy sauce or gluten-free tsuyu is indicated.
Vegan dishes are listed but marked as not yet on sale pending ingredients, and they would be prepared in a kitchen that handles fish dashi and meat, so cross-contact is likely; confirm by phone.
The menu does include a small vegan section (keema curry udon/rice and soy-milk carbonara udon) plus mountain-vegetable udon and vegetable tempura, showing some plant-based intent.

name: うな菊 奈良本店 (Unakiku Nara Honten)

claims.text: The signature tare is made by blending pure Tenno Shoyu soy sauce with hon-mirin; standard Japanese soy sauce is brewed with wheat, so the eel glaze contains gluten.
This is a dedicated eel restaurant; effectively every dish is built around grilled freshwater eel, so there is no plant-based mainline and shared grill/tare make it unsuitable for vegans.
